claim.quote: We currently hold the world record for the highest instantaneous luminosity ever achieved at a particle accelerator: 5.319 x 1034 cm−2s−1 achieved on June 30, 2026.

date.note: The date is the day the record luminosity was achieved ('achieved on June 30, 2026'), as stated by the Belle II collaboration on its own home page (read 2026-09-16); it is not an announcement date, but date_kind has no other value that fits a technology milestone.

name: SuperKEKB world-record instantaneous luminosity
notes: Earlier values from other sources: 2.22 × 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹ on 15 June 2020 (KEK IPNS release, https://www2.kek.jp/ipns/en/release/20200626/: "At 20:34 on 15th June 2020, SuperKEKB achieved the world’s highest instantaneous luminosity for a colliding-beam accelerator, setting a record of 2.22×1034 cm-2 s-1.") and a peak of 5.1 × 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹ (Belle II input to the 2025 European Strategy update, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.24155: "SuperKEKB reached a peak luminosity of 5.1×1034 cm−2 s−1"). These are separate records, not recorded as separate results.

summary.plain: The Belle II collaboration states that SuperKEKB, the electron-positron collider in Tsukuba, Japan, holds the world record for the highest instantaneous luminosity ever achieved at a particle accelerator: 5.319 × 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹, achieved on 30 June 2026. Instantaneous luminosity measures how many particle collisions the beams deliver per second.
summary.technical: SuperKEKB reached a peak instantaneous luminosity of 5.319 × 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹ on 30 June 2026, which the Belle II collaboration states is the highest ever achieved at a particle accelerator. Earlier values from other sources are in the notes (2.22 × 10³⁴ on 15 June 2020; 5.1 × 10³⁴ quoted in March 2025). The Belle II input to the 2025 European Strategy update describes the machine's novel nano-beam scheme, based on a large horizontal crossing angle.

title: World record for the highest instantaneous luminosity ever achieved at a particle accelerator
why_it_matters: Instantaneous luminosity is the collision rate the machine delivers to the Belle II detector. The Belle II input to the 2025 European Strategy update states a plan to reach a peak luminosity of 1.0 × 10³⁵ cm⁻² s⁻¹ by 2026 and an integrated luminosity of 50 ab⁻¹; the 2026 record, 5.319 × 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹, is below that peak-luminosity goal.
